title: Crossing increases vigour; close interbreeding decreases it

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Crossing increases vigour; close interbreeding decreases it

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In animals and plants, crosses between different varieties or between different strains of the same variety give vigour and fertility to the offspring, while close interbreeding reduces vigour and fertility.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: a cross between different varieties, or between individuals of the same variety but of another strain, gives vigour and fertility to the offspring; and on the other hand, that _close_ interbreeding diminishes vigour and fertility

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species”. Scope: animals and plants, wild and domestic

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.77

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The outcomes and comparison groups are direct and experimentally discriminating. Many public datasets exist, but a broad synthesis would still cover only a biased subset of wild and domestic organisms.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Meta-analyse controlled crosses at graded genetic distances for offspring survival, growth, fertility and reproductive output. Higher performance after moderate outcrossing and lower performance after close inbreeding support the claim; flat or opposite average effects refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Outbreeding depression can occur at large genetic distances.

Crossing experiments are unevenly distributed among taxa and traits.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.94
discriminating power: 0.82
data adequacy: 0.62
analysis feasibility: 0.76
data existence: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Inbreeding coefficient and fitness components are standard variables, and the confirming pattern is a negative relationship between relatedness of mates and offspring performance. The measurements exist in volume for domesticates and for a smaller set of wild species, but they must be compiled from studies. Once compiled, the contrast is fairly discriminating, with known biological confounds that meta-analysis can partially address.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare vigour and fertility among offspring of crosses between varieties or strains and offspring of close inbred matings, using inbreeding coefficient as the predictor. Higher fitness of the crosses, and lower fitness as inbreeding increases, would confirm the contrast; no relationship, or a reversal after maternal effects are removed, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Wild populations are less completely measured than livestock and cultivated plants.

Fitness of crosses versus close matings is published experiment by experiment rather than in one open database.

Maternal effects, purging, and heterosis specific to crops can inflate the apparent benefit of crossing.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.52
analysis feasibility: 0.52
discriminating power: 0.7
